# Proof Summary: Death of Elijah Wilkins (born circa 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky)

## Research Question

When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born circa 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Conclusion

The preponderance of available evidence strongly suggests that Elijah Wilkins died after 1870 and before the 1885 term of the Muhlenberg County Court — in or near Muhlenberg County, Kentucky. No Kentucky death certificate exists for him: statewide death registration did not begin until 1911, and Wilkins was last documented alive in the 1870 federal census, placing his death decades before that requirement took effect. An exact date and cause of death cannot be established from the records searched to date. The bounded bracket (after 1870, before 1885) is the most precise conclusion the current evidence supports.

## Evidence

The sole substantive source is the Muhlenberg County Court Order Books, a derivative source (a full-text index of the original county order-book pages; the original order book was not separately imaged in this search). A 1885 term entry records the grant of administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, with Jesse Wilkins named administrator.¹

The record supplies **secondary information**: the county court clerk recorded the administration grant at a remove from the actual facts of Elijah's death, and the clerk's proximity to those facts is unknown. The evidence is **indirect**: the record establishes that Elijah was dead by the 1885 court term but states no death date or cause.

## Identity of the Decedent

The decedent named in the estate record is identified as the subject (Elijah Wilkins, I1) on two grounds. First, the name "Elijah Wilkins" in Muhlenberg County matches the subject's known name and county of continuous residence through 1870. Second, and more compellingly, Jesse Wilkins — the subject's documented son — served as administrator of the estate (a_003). Under Kentucky intestate practice, close kin were customarily preferred as administrators; Jesse's appointment to administer an intestate Muhlenberg County estate in 1885 strongly corroborates that this is his father's estate rather than that of an unrelated Elijah Wilkins.

## Death Bracket

**Lower bound — 1870 federal census:** Elijah Wilkins is documented residing in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, in the 1870 federal census (recorded in the project tree as a prior-research Residence fact). This establishes he was alive as of that enumeration.

**Upper bound — 1885 estate administration:** The Muhlenberg County Court granted administration of his estate during the 1885 term, establishing he was deceased by that point (a_001).

Together these two records bracket the death to **after 1870 and before 1885**.

## Documented Negative: No Kentucky Death Certificate

Kentucky did not begin statewide death registration until 1911. Elijah Wilkins's death, occurring in the 1870s or early 1880s, predates that registration system by decades, so **no death certificate exists for him**. A search of Kentucky Deaths collections on FamilySearch (12 results examined) returned no record for the subject. This negative result is fully expected and constitutes a **documented absence**, not a research gap.

| Name, Elijah Wilkins (a_002) | Derivative | Secondary | Direct |
| Jesse as administrator (a_003) | Derivative | Secondary | Indirect |

## Research Scope and Limitations

Two record types were searched in this phase: (1) Kentucky statewide death collections — negative, as anticipated given the 1911 registration start — and (2) Muhlenberg County probate records — positive, yielding the 1885 estate entry. The following record types were **not searched** and could potentially refine or corroborate the bracket: Muhlenberg County deed records and annual tax lists for 1871–1884 (a disappearance from the tax rolls would help narrow the bracket), county cemetery transcriptions, and church burial registers. Research has not been declared exhaustive. The exact death date remains open pending further search.

### The Online Claim

An unsourced FamilySearch Family Tree entry, copied into several descendant trees without independent corroboration, names Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary (born approximately 1800), as the father of Patrick Flynn (born approximately 1845 in Pennsylvania). No record is cited by any tree carrying this assertion.

The 1850 U.S. Federal Census places Patrick Flynn, age five, in the household of Bridget Flynn (widow), Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, corroborating a birth year of approximately 1845 in Ireland.[^1] An age of five in 1850 implies birth no earlier than approximately 1843 and most plausibly approximately 1845. Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (no. 4521) records his death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, at age approximately sixty-three — independently placing his birth at approximately 1845.[^2] The certificate's informant, James Brown (a son-in-law), provided secondary information on the birth year, derived from reported age at death; the attending physician provided primary information on the death date. Both original records are consistent and convergent on a birth year of approximately 1845.

The 1850 census household is headed by Bridget Flynn as a widow, with no adult male Flynn present, indicating Patrick's father was already absent — dead, or separated from the family — by 1850.

### Identifying Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry

The Ballingarry (County Tipperary) Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842, at approximately age forty-two, survived by his wife Bridget.[^3] This entry was recorded by the officiating priest contemporaneously: an original source bearing primary information about Thomas Flynn's death. The identifying details — townland (Ballingarry), approximate age, and wife named Bridget — match, in their entirety, the Thomas Flynn the online tree names as Patrick's father, establishing that this is the same individual the claim refers to.

### The Chronological Impossibility

Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry died, at the latest, in November 1842. Patrick Flynn was born at the earliest approximately 1843 (allowing for census age error) and most plausibly approximately 1845. A man who died in November 1842 cannot have fathered a child born in 1843 or later. The gap between Thomas's confirmed death and Patrick's earliest plausible birth is irreconcilable — the hypothesis is chronologically impossible.

The online tree's claim is accordingly **disproved** by primary-information, original-source evidence — not merely unsupported.

### Research Scope and Limitations

Three record types were searched for this question: the 1850 U.S. Federal Census (Schuylkill County), the Ballingarry (County Tipperary) Catholic parish burial registers, and Pennsylvania death certificates (1908). Research has not been declared exhaustive. Additional record types bearing on Patrick Flynn's actual parentage — including Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, early-nineteenth-century Tipperary parish baptism registers, passenger lists, and Pennsylvania naturalisation records — remain to be searched. None of those gaps affect the disproof: the chronological impossibility established by the burial register entry holds regardless of what further research may reveal. The 1908 death certificate does not name Patrick's father, consistent with a son-in-law informant who lacked that personal knowledge.

### Conclusion

The preponderance of primary evidence disproves the hypothesis that Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary (buried 14 November 1842), was the father of Patrick Flynn (born approximately 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania). The Thomas Flynn the online tree names was interred nearly three years before Patrick's birth. This claim originated in an unsourced online family tree and was propagated without corroborating evidence. It is chronologically impossible and is **disproved**.

# Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry Was Not the Father of Patrick Flynn

**Proof Summary — Disproved**

## Research Question

Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary (born about 1800), the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? The claim originates from an unsourced FamilySearch Family Tree entry copied across several online trees without any supporting record.

## Evidence

Three original records — the 1850 U.S. Federal Census, the Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register, and Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate — collectively establish the dates and identities that resolve this question.

**Patrick Flynn's birth, about 1845.** The 1850 U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, records Patrick Flynn as age 5 in the household of widow Bridget Flynn, placing his birth approximately 1845 in Ireland.¹ The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate for Patrick Flynn corroborates this figure: it gives his age at death as approximately 63, producing a calculated birth year of approximately 1845.² The death certificate informant was James Brown, his son-in-law — a family member not present at the birth, providing secondary information derived from a reported age. That his derived birth year precisely matches the census record strengthens the reliability of the ~1845 figure. Even allowing for a year or two of census age rounding, no evidence places Patrick's birth any earlier than approximately 1843.

**Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry's burial, 14 November 1842.** The Ballingarry, County Tipperary, Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842.³ The entry was recorded by the officiating priest at the time of interment — an original source carrying primary information. It identifies the deceased by townland (Ballingarry), approximate age (about 42), and wife (Bridget), all of which match the identifiers the online tree associates with the supposed father. This is the Thomas Flynn the online tree claim refers to.

## Analysis and Correlation

The chronological relationship between these dates is decisive. Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was buried on 14 November 1842. Patrick Flynn was born approximately 1845 — roughly three years after Thomas's burial. The burial register entry is primary information from an official witness; the birth year rests on two independent, corroborating estimates that agree within census-age rounding error. A man cannot father a child he predeceased by three years. The claimed parentage is chronologically impossible.

The online tree claim carries no evidential weight. It cites no record, and an authored, unsourced digital tree does not constitute independent evidence — one unsupported assertion copied across multiple trees remains a single unverified claim regardless of how widely it circulates.

## Conclusion

The claim that Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, was the father of Patrick Flynn (born ~1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania) is **disproved**. The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register — an original source with primary information from the officiating priest — establishes that Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was buried on 14 November 1842, approximately three years before Patrick Flynn was born. The parentage claim is chronologically impossible and originates from an unsourced online tree without record support.

The identity of Patrick Flynn's actual father remains an open research question. It has not been addressed by the evidence gathered to date and will require additional searches: other U.S. census years (1860–1900), naturalization or passenger records, Irish baptism registers for a Patrick Flynn born ~1845, and Schuylkill County church records could collectively narrow or identify his parentage.

---

² Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026.

³ Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Correlation is well-handled:** The narrative correctly identifies that two censuses provide independent, contemporaneous corroboration through co-enumeration (indirect), while the death certificate provides a direct naming of the father from a secondary informant. Grouping these as "three independent lines of evidence" is accurate — the 1850 and 1860 census images are from different enumerators and different years; the death certificate is a wholly different record type and informant.

**One analytical note worth flagging:** The narrative notes that the two census informants were "likely the same household member (Thomas Flynn or his wife)" in the conflict section but doesn't carry this observation into the parentage analysis. If both census co-enumeration assertions ultimately trace to the same real-world informant (Thomas himself), they are not fully independent for the parentage inference. The narrative should acknowledge this partial dependence. At the Probable tier it doesn't invalidate the conclusion, but it slightly overstates the independence of the corroborating lines.

---

### GPS Component 4 — Resolution of Conflicting Evidence

**Assessment: Well met.**

c_001 (birthplace: Ireland vs. Pennsylvania) is the only recorded conflict, and it is `resolved`. The narrative's Conflict Resolution section satisfies all four required steps:

1. **Acknowledges the conflict explicitly:** "A birthplace conflict exists" — stated ✓
2. **Analyzes reliability of each side:** contemporary recordings vs. 63-year-later recollection; household informant proximity vs. son-in-law secondary informant — analyzed ✓
3. **Explains which is more credible and why:** "Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants" — explained ✓
4. **Provides a plausible explanation for the error:** son-in-law "may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his place of birth, or may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland before immigrating as a young child" — explained ✓

Importantly, the proof correctly characterizes this as a **collateral conflict** (about birthplace, not parentage). It does not raise the conflict to a tier-capping level (Possible), which would only be warranted if the conflict disputed the concluded relationship itself. This judgment is sound.

---

### GPS Component 5 — Soundly Reasoned, Coherently Written Conclusion

**Assessment: Substantially met; two organizational observations.**

**What the narrative does well:**
- The conclusion is stated at the top ("Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania") — question and answer both identifiable ✓
- Phrasing is consistently conditional throughout ("probably," "consistent with," "support a parent-child relationship") — appropriate for the Probable tier ✓
- The Assessment section transparently states why Proved is not warranted and what would advance the tier ✓
- The Conflict Resolution section is a distinct, clearly labeled section ✓

**Observation 1 — Organization follows research chronology, not significance.** The GPS writing reference states "the best presentation order is almost never the order in which you collected evidence." The narrative presents sources in the order they were found (1850, 1860, death cert). A significance-based or reasoning-chain order would introduce the strongest piece first — here, the death certificate's explicit naming of Thomas Flynn as father — and then show how the two census records independently corroborate it. Reversing the presentation order would make the conclusion more rhetorically persuasive. This doesn't impair correctness at the Probable tier, but it is a structural weakness.

**Observation 2 — Thomas Flynn's identity as a specific individual is understated.** The narrative identifies the father as "Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania" but does not fully distinguish him as a specific person (e.g., approximate birth year ~1818, born Ireland, head of dwelling 84 in 1850 and dwelling 112 in 1860). For a proof naming a specific parent, the conclusion should give the reader enough detail to identify that parent uniquely. Person_evidence pe_003 links the a_005 name assertion to I2 with a `match_score: 0.82`, but that reasoning doesn't surface in the narrative.

**Overall Component 5 verdict:** The logic chain is sound and followable. The tier is stated, the rationale is disclosed, phrasing matches the tier. The two structural observations above are improvements for a future revision, not errors that undermine the current conclusion.

---

### Overall Verdict

**ps_001 stands as a sound Probable-tier proof on the evidence it cites.** The tier is correctly calibrated: three independent lines of evidence converge on Thomas Flynn as father, but two of three are indirect (household co-enumeration, no pre-1880 relationship column) and the sole direct naming comes from a secondary informant (son-in-law). entry.narrative_markdown:
## When and Where Anders Monsen Married Unna Halsteinsdatter

**Research question:** When and where did Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) marry Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX)?

**Conclusion:** The preponderance of available evidence strongly suggests that Anders Monsen married Unna Halsteinsdatter on **25 June 1786** at **Hamre, Hordaland, Norway**.

### Evidence

The sole source for this event is an entry in the FamilySearch indexed database for Norwegian church-book marriages: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register.

This source is a **derivative** record — an indexed database entry citing the original Hamre prestegjeld parish register (kirkeboker) rather than the register itself. The information it records — the marriage date, the place, and the names of the contracting parties — is **primary**: it derives from a register entry made at or near the time of the marriage by the officiating minister or parish clerk acting in an official capacity (informant proximity: official duty). The evidence is **direct**: the record explicitly identifies Anders Monsen as the groom and states that the marriage took place on 25 June 1786 at Hamre.

The bride's name appears in the FamilySearch index as "Urna Halsteinsdr," a transcription variant of "Unna Halsteinsdatter." The variation is minor: *Urna* for *Unna* is a common indexer transcription error, and the abbreviation of *datter* (daughter) to *dr* is a standard convention in Norwegian parish-register indexes. Unna Halsteinsdatter's christening record (27 May 1745, Hamre, Hordaland) independently corroborates the name and confirms her association with the same parish. The pre-existing Couple relationship linking LKFW-9XH to KZHH-VTX in the family tree is consistent with this identification. No conflicting evidence was found.

### Research Scope

For a marriage in 1786 Norway, the church parish register is the only contemporaneous record type. Civil marriage registration did not begin in Norway until 1875; no parallel state record, newspaper announcement, or alternative ecclesiastical source for this event and jurisdiction plausibly exists. ## Who Was the Father of Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: Not Proved**

Despite a reasonably exhaustive search of the available record base, Patrick Flynn's father cannot be identified from the evidence in hand. Two candidate fathers exist in the 1850 census, but the bridging records that could distinguish between them — or connect adult Patrick to either household — have been searched and do not supply that connection.

### The Subject

Patrick Flynn was born in Ireland about 1845 and settled in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, where he worked as a coal laborer. He appears in the 1860 federal census as a 15-year-old boarder in the household of Owen Donnelly, Schuylkill County.[^1] He died in Schuylkill County on 12 March 1908.[^2] His death certificate (no. 4521), completed by his son-in-law James Brown, leaves the father's name blank; Brown reported the father as "unknown."[^2]

### Candidate Household A: Thomas Flynn

The 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County records a Patrick Flynn, age 5, born in Ireland, in the household of Thomas Flynn, head (dwelling 84, family 91).[^3] The age and birthplace are consistent with the subject. However, the 1850 census does not state relationships — Patrick's position in the household as a child of Thomas Flynn is inferred from household structure, not recorded by the enumerator. The informant is unknown. Classified as: original source; indeterminate information (informant identity and proximity unknown); indirect evidence (co-residence inference, not a statement of parentage).

### Candidate Household B: Michael Flynn

The same census also records a Patrick Flynn, age 6, born in Ireland, in the household of Michael Flynn, head (dwelling 210, family 233), in a different enumeration district of Schuylkill County.[^4] An age of 6 in 1850 implies birth about 1844 — within the normal margin of census age error for a subject born about 1845. The same classification applies: original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence. This candidate is equally plausible as the Thomas household.

### Bridging Evidence: The 1860 Census

The critical test is whether the 1860 census can connect adult Patrick to either 1850 household. It cannot. In 1860 Patrick appears as a boarder in the Donnelly household, living and working with no Flynn adult present, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor in that enumeration.[^1] The record confirms Patrick's residence in Schuylkill County but provides no backward link to either 1850 household.

### Negative Evidence: The Death Certificate

The 1908 death certificate is the record most likely to name the father directly. It does not. Informant James Brown (son-in-law) stated the father was "unknown," leaving the field blank.[^2] Brown is a secondary informant on Patrick's parentage — a family member not personally present at the relevant events — and his ignorance of the grandfather's name carries weight: it suggests that the father's identity was not passed down within Patrick's family.

### Why Neither Candidate Can Be Favored

Both candidate households offer precisely the same evidentiary base: one indirect inference from co-residence in an 1850 census that does not record relationships. Neither candidate has any additional corroboration — no church record, no 1860 co-residence, no family document — that would distinguish it from the other. The 1860 census, the death certificate, and the Catholic parish register search all fail to supply a distinguishing link. The two hypotheses (h_001: Thomas Flynn; h_002: Michael Flynn) are evidentiary equals, and selecting one over the other would require inventing a preference the evidence does not support.

### Scope of Research and Remaining Avenues

The following record types were searched: (1) 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County; (2) 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County; (3) Pennsylvania death certificates (1908); and (4) FamilySearch and NLI Catholic Parish Registers for a Patrick Flynn baptism in Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843–1850. No baptism naming a father was located. Records that could yet resolve the question include an unindexed church register, a family Bible record, or an 1870–1880 census trace of Thomas and Michael Flynn in Schuylkill County — the latter might reveal whether either man remained in proximity to adult Patrick and could provide a circumstantial link. That trace was not pursued within the current research plan.

### Conclusion

Patrick Flynn's father is not proved by the available evidence. Two candidates — Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, 1850 Schuylkill County census) and Michael Flynn (dwelling 210, 1850 Schuylkill County census) — are supported by equal and identical indirect evidence and neither can be eliminated. No record connects adult Patrick to either household, and his death certificate records the father as unknown. The question remains open pending discovery of a baptism record, Bible record, or other document naming Patrick's father directly.

## Who Was the Father of Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion: Not Proved**

Despite a reasonably exhaustive search of the available record base, Patrick Flynn's father cannot be identified from the evidence in hand. Two candidate fathers exist in the 1850 census, but the bridging records that could distinguish between them — or connect adult Patrick to either household — have been searched and do not supply that connection.

### The Subject

Patrick Flynn was born in Ireland about 1845 and settled in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, where he worked as a coal laborer. He appears in the 1860 federal census as a 15-year-old boarder in the household of Owen Donnelly, Schuylkill County.[^1] He died in Schuylkill County on 12 March 1908.[^2] His death certificate (no. 4521), completed by his son-in-law James Brown, leaves the father's name blank; Brown reported the father as "unknown."[^2]

### Candidate Household A: Thomas Flynn

The 1850 federal census for Schuylkill County records a Patrick Flynn, age 5, born in Ireland, in the household of Thomas Flynn, head (dwelling 84, family 91).[^3] The age and birthplace are consistent with the subject. However, the 1850 census does not state relationships — Patrick's position in the household as a child of Thomas Flynn is inferred from household structure, not recorded by the enumerator. The informant is unknown. Classified as: original source; indeterminate information (informant identity and proximity unknown); indirect evidence (co-residence inference, not a statement of parentage).

### Candidate Household B: Michael Flynn

The same census also records a Patrick Flynn, age 6, born in Ireland, in the household of Michael Flynn, head (dwelling 210, family 233), in a different enumeration district of Schuylkill County.[^4] An age of 6 in 1850 implies birth about 1844 — within the normal margin of census age error for a subject born about 1845. The same classification applies: original source; indeterminate information; indirect evidence. This candidate is equally plausible as the Thomas household.

### Bridging Evidence: The 1860 Census

The critical test is whether the 1860 census can connect adult Patrick to either 1850 household. It cannot. In 1860 Patrick appears as a boarder in the Donnelly household, living and working with no Flynn adult present, and neither Thomas nor Michael Flynn appears as a near neighbor in that enumeration.[^1] The record confirms Patrick's residence in Schuylkill County but provides no backward link to either 1850 household.

### Negative Evidence: The Death Certificate

The 1908 death certificate is the record most likely to name the father directly. It does not. Informant James Brown (son-in-law) stated the father was "unknown," leaving the field blank.[^2] Brown is a secondary informant on Patrick's parentage — a family member not personally present at the relevant events — and his ignorance of the grandfather's name carries weight: it suggests that the father's identity was not passed down within Patrick's family.

### Why Neither Candidate Can Be Favored

Both candidate households offer precisely the same evidentiary base: one indirect inference from co-residence in an 1850 census that does not record relationships. Neither candidate has any additional corroboration — no church record, no 1860 co-residence, no family document — that would distinguish it from the other. The 1860 census, the death certificate, and the Catholic parish register search all fail to supply a distinguishing link. The two hypotheses (h_001: Thomas Flynn; h_002: Michael Flynn) are evidentiary equals, and selecting one over the other would require inventing a preference the evidence does not support.

### Scope of Research and Remaining Avenues

The following record types were searched: (1) 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County; (2) 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County; (3) Pennsylvania death certificates (1908); and (4) FamilySearch and NLI Catholic Parish Registers for a Patrick Flynn baptism in Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843–1850. No baptism naming a father was located. Records that could yet resolve the question include an unindexed church register, a family Bible record, or an 1870–1880 census trace of Thomas and Michael Flynn in Schuylkill County — the latter might reveal whether either man remained in proximity to adult Patrick and could provide a circumstantial link. That trace was not pursued within the current research plan.

### Conclusion

Patrick Flynn's father is not proved by the available evidence. Two candidates — Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, 1850 Schuylkill County census) and Michael Flynn (dwelling 210, 1850 Schuylkill County census) — are supported by equal and identical indirect evidence and neither can be eliminated. No record connects adult Patrick to either household, and his death certificate records the father as unknown. The question remains open pending discovery of a baptism record, Bible record, or other document naming Patrick's father directly.

# Who Was the Father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, Ireland; d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

## Proof Summary

**Conclusion:** The evidence conclusively establishes that Patrick Flynn — born approximately 1845 in Ireland and died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — is the son of **Thomas Flynn**.

---

### Primary Evidence: Two Independent Original Sources with Primary Information

Two original, fully independent sources provide primary information that directly names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father.

**1845 Catholic Baptismal Register.** The baptismal register of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, County Tipperary, Ireland, records the baptism of Patricius Flynn on 12 March 1845, naming Thomas Flynn and Maria Brennan as parents.¹ The entry was recorded by the officiating priest, Rev. Michael O'Connor, in the presence of the parents and godparents. This is an *original* source; the parentage information is *primary* (the priest and the parents themselves are contemporary witnesses to the ceremony); and the evidence is *direct* (the entry names the father explicitly). The 1845 baptismal register carries the highest evidentiary weight in this inquiry.

**Flynn Family Bible.** The birth and family record pages of a Flynn family Bible (Dublin imprint, 1840) record Patrick Flynn, born 1845, as the son of Thomas Flynn and Mary Brennan.² The entries are in a single consistent contemporaneous hand, and the 1840 imprint predates all entries — supporting that births were recorded as events occurred rather than reconstructed later. The identified recorder is the father, Thomas Flynn, who had firsthand knowledge of his children's births. This source is *original*; the parentage information is *primary*; and the evidence is *direct*. It is fully independent of the baptismal register (different recorder, different record type, different country of origin), constituting a second primary-information source on the parent-child relationship.

---

### Corroborating Evidence: Three Additional Original Sources

Three further original sources corroborate the parentage through indirect or secondary evidence.

**1850 U.S. Census.** Patrick Flynn, age 5 (born Ireland), appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, head, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 84, family 91.³ The 1850 census did not enumerate relationships; the parent-child association is inferred from co-residence, shared surname, and household position. The source is *original*; the census enumerator's identity of the co-resident household is *primary* for residence; and the parentage inference is *indirect* evidence. The census confirms Patrick's childhood residence in Thomas Flynn's home and establishes the Pennsylvania context.

**1860 U.S. Census.** Patrick Flynn, age 15 (born Ireland), again appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, head, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, dwelling 112, family 119.⁴ As with the 1850 census, the relationship is inferred from household structure; neither enumeration states relationships explicitly. The source is *original*; the parentage inference is *indirect*. Consistent co-residence across two enumeration years, a decade apart, strengthens the parent-child identification.

**1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate.** The death certificate of Patrick Flynn (certificate no. 4521, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County) names Thomas Flynn as father.⁵ The informant was son-in-law James Brown. This source is *original*; the parentage information is *secondary* (Brown is reporting what he was told about events predating his connection to the family); and the evidence is *direct* (the certificate names the father). The secondary informant status reduces the weight of this record for parentage purposes relative to the baptismal register and family Bible, but it independently names Thomas Flynn and is consistent with all other sources.

---

### Conflict Resolution

One conflict was identified and resolved. The 1850 and 1860 censuses record Patrick's birthplace as Ireland,³ ⁴ while the 1908 death certificate records it as Pennsylvania.⁵ This conflict does not bear on the parentage question — all sources agree that Thomas Flynn is the father — but it was analyzed and resolved nonetheless. Ireland is accepted as the correct birthplace: the census records were made when Patrick was a child and reflect information closer to the birth event, while the death certificate informant (a son-in-law) was a secondary source for birth facts decades removed and may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his birthplace. The 1845 Irish baptismal register independently corroborates Ireland as the birthplace.¹

---

### Research Scope

Searches were conducted on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and MyHeritage for U.S. census records (1850 and 1860, Schuylkill County); FamilySearch for Pennsylvania vital records (1908 death certificate) and Schuylkill County probate records (1870–1890); and the National Library of Ireland digital Catholic Parish Registers for a Patrick Flynn baptism in County Tipperary (1844–1846). The Flynn family Bible was examined from digital images provided by a descendant. A probate search for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (1870–1890) returned no records — a negative finding consistent with dying intestate, dying outside the county, or a name variation; the absence does not contradict the parentage conclusion. No additional plausible repositories were identified for Schuylkill County records of this era or the relevant Irish parish registers.

---

### Conclusion

Thomas Flynn is proved to be the father of Patrick Flynn. Two independent original sources carry primary information directly naming Thomas Flynn as the father: the 1845 Irish Catholic baptismal register recorded by the officiating priest in the presence of the parents, and the contemporaneous Flynn family Bible birth entry recorded by the father himself. These are corroborated by two original sources establishing Patrick's decade-long childhood co-residence in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (1850 and 1860 censuses), and a death certificate whose informant independently named Thomas Flynn as father. The single identified conflict (Patrick's birthplace) does not bear on the parentage conclusion and has been resolved in favor of Ireland. All five components of the Genealogical Proof Standard are satisfied: reasonably exhaustive research has been conducted and declared; all factual claims are fully cited to identified sources; each source and piece of evidence has been analyzed and classified; the identified conflict has been resolved; and this conclusion is soundly reasoned and coherently written. As with all genealogical conclusions, newly discovered evidence could require reassessment, but the current record set supports a finding of proved.

# Who Was the Father of Patrick Flynn (born ~1845; died 12 March 1908)?

## Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence strongly suggests that **Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania was the father of Patrick Flynn** (born approximately 1845 in Ireland; died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania). Three independent sources corroborate this conclusion; no competing candidate has been identified.

## Evidence

**1850 U.S. Census — Household Co-enumeration (indirect evidence)**

The 1850 U.S. federal population schedule for Schuylkill County enumerated Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, in dwelling 84, family 91, headed by Thomas Flynn.¹ The 1850 census did not record household relationships; the father-son inference rests on shared surname, household position, and an age differential consistent with parentage (Thomas approximately age 32, Patrick age 5). This is **indirect evidence** of parentage from an **original** source; information quality is **indeterminate** because the identity of the reporting informant cannot be determined from the census. An Ancestry.com derivative index of the same census independently confirms the same household placement but adds no additional evidentiary weight.²

**1860 U.S. Census — Continued Co-enumeration (indirect evidence)**

Ten years later, the 1860 U.S. federal population schedule for Schuylkill County again enumerated Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, in dwelling 112, family 119, headed by Thomas Flynn.³ The 1860 schedule likewise did not record household relationships (that column was not added until 1880). The repeated co-enumeration of the same individuals in the same county — with ages advancing by approximately ten years between enumerations — substantially strengthens the parent-child inference. This is **indirect evidence** from an **original** source with **indeterminate** information quality.

**1908 Death Certificate — Father Named Directly (direct evidence, secondary information)**

Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (no. 4521) records Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father.⁴ This is **direct evidence** of parentage from an **original** source. However, the informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law — a person with no firsthand knowledge of Patrick's own parentage. Brown's statement is therefore **secondary information**. While secondary informants can be correct, their testimony carries less evidentiary weight than that of a witness with firsthand knowledge. The death certificate is nonetheless significant: it is an independently compiled, contemporaneous official record in which a close family member identified Thomas Flynn as the father, consistent with both census placements.

## Birthplace Discrepancy — Resolved

The death certificate records Patrick's birthplace as Pennsylvania, while both census records give Ireland (conflict c_001). The discrepancy is attributable to the son-in-law informant's lack of firsthand knowledge of Patrick's origins: Patrick likely immigrated as a young child, and Brown may have conflated Patrick's long-term Pennsylvania residence with his birthplace. The two census records — made closer in time to the birth event and by informants more likely to have household knowledge of origins — outweigh the later, secondary recollection. Ireland is accepted as Patrick's birthplace.

## Mother

No record gathered to date names Patrick Flynn's mother. Census records before 1880 did not enumerate household relationships, making it impossible from the household listings alone to determine which adult female in the Thomas Flynn household (if any) was Patrick's mother. The mother's identity is an open research question. Records that could establish her identity include the 1870 and 1880 census enumerations for Thomas Flynn's household (which would show the mother's name and age if she survived to those dates), Irish Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County (likely St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville), and Thomas Flynn's naturalization records — none of which have yet been searched.

## Research Scope and Limitations

Searches conducted include the 1850 U.S. census on FamilySearch (original) and Ancestry.com (derivative), the 1860 U.S. census on FamilySearch (original), and Patrick's 1908 death certificate on FamilySearch (original). Research has not been declared exhaustive for q_001. Unsearched record types bearing on the parentage question include Thomas Flynn's probate records (search in progress), the 1870 and 1880 census enumerations for Thomas Flynn's household, Irish Catholic church registers, and naturalization records. These gaps preclude a proved conclusion.

## Tier

The conclusion is rated **probable**. All three independent sources are consistent with Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, no competing candidate appears in any record gathered, and the resolved birthplace conflict pertains to a collateral fact rather than to the identity of the father. The tier is held at probable rather than proved because (1) research is not declared exhaustive and (2) the census parentage assertions rest on indirect evidence (inferred household position) rather than explicit relationship statements. Thomas Flynn's probate records and the 1870–1880 census enumerations for his household are the highest-priority next steps that could advance the tier.
